chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Yazid ibn Ishaq, from Harun ibn Hamza al-Ghanawi, from Hariz, from Abu Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

'Whichever man who has a dispute with a (believing) brother of his regarding a right, and then invites him to a man from his (believing) brethren to judge between them, but he refuses — except to have the matter raised to those (unjust judges) — he is at the status of those

about whom God Mighty and Majestic said: 'Have you not seen those who allege that they believe in what was revealed to you and what was revealed before you? They desire to seek judgment from the taghut, though they were commanded to deny it' — the Verse.

key_terms.الطَّاغُوتِ: taghut — tyrant, false deity, unjust authority
key_terms.يُرَافِعَهُ: to raise/take a case against someone in court

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Sadiq say about Muslims who take disputes to unjust judges?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) issues a sharp ruling that a Muslim who, despite being offered arbitration by a fellow believer, insists on taking his dispute to unjust (non-Islamic) courts is equated with the hypocrites condemned in Quran 4:60. This teaching comes in the context of early Islamic jurisprudence, where the Imams sought to preserve Muslim communal autonomy by directing disputes to their own scholarly arbiters rather than the Abbasid state courts or other non-Islamic authorities. The term 'taghut' historically referred to pre-Islamic oracles, but in this context applies broadly to any authority that rules other than by divine law.
word_analysis: he take the case against him
